cards.front: What is the difference between JAVA_HOME and PATH?
cards.back: JAVA_HOME names the JDK directory, used by tools like Maven and Gradle; PATH lets the shell find java and javac
cards.extra: Build tools read JAVA_HOME to locate the compiler; the shell uses PATH. Setting one and not the other is the classic "mvn uses a different JDK" bug.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::13 JVM and Tooling::03 Core JDK Tools

cards.front: What is the difference between classpath and build path?
cards.back: Build path is what the IDE/compiler uses to compile; classpath is what the JVM uses at run time
cards.extra: They are configured separately and can disagree — which is why code compiles in the IDE and fails with NoClassDefFoundError from the command line.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::13 JVM and Tooling::03 Core JDK Tools

cards.front: What is the difference between -sourcepath and -classpath?
cards.back: sourcepath tells javac where to find .java sources; classpath points at compiled .class files and jars
cards.extra: javac compiles sources it finds via sourcepath on demand; classpath entries are used as-is.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::13 JVM and Tooling::03 Core JDK Tools

cards.front: How do you derive a UUID from a string?
cards.back: UUID.nameUUIDFromBytes(bytes) — deterministic, version 3 (MD5-based)
cards.extra: Same input, same UUID, forever. Version 5 (SHA-1) is not in the JDK; it needs a library.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::13 JVM and Tooling::03 Core JDK Tools

cards.front: Does an enum's toString() affect valueOf?
cards.back: No — valueOf matches name(), which is final and is the declared identifier
cards.extra: Overriding toString for display is fine, but round-tripping through valueOf(toString()) then breaks.

cards.front: What are the five ways to create an object in Java?
cards.back: new, reflection, clone(), deserialization, and a factory method
cards.extra: The last four bypass the constructor you can see, which is why they are also the ways to get an object in an invalid state.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::01 Classes and Objects

cards.front: What does Project Panama bring to Java?
cards.back: The Foreign Function & Memory API — calling native code and managing off-heap memory without JNI
cards.extra: It replaces hand-written C glue: Linker, MemorySegment and FunctionDescriptor are the entry points.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::13 JVM and Tooling::03 Core JDK Tools

cards.front: How does a record differ from a final class?
cards.back: A record gives you components, accessors, equals, hashCode and toString from one declaration; a final class only blocks subclassing
cards.extra: Both prevent extension. A record also documents that it is a transparent data carrier — and it cannot declare extra instance fields.

cards.front: What is structured concurrency (JEP 428)?
cards.back: A scope, StructuredTaskScope, in which subtasks are forked and all complete — or are cancelled — before the scope exits
cards.extra: It makes task lifetimes follow the block structure, so a failed subtask cancels its siblings instead of leaking threads.

cards.front: What is a record pattern?
cards.back: Destructuring a record in a type test: if (o instanceof Point(int x, int y)) — preview in Java 19, standard in 21
cards.extra: It binds the components directly, removing the accessor calls and the nested instanceof chain.

cards.front: How does String... differ from String[] in a signature?
cards.back: String... accepts zero or more arguments at the call site; String[] requires an array
cards.extra: Both compile to an array parameter, so the two overloads cannot coexist — they clash.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::02 Attributes and Methods

cards.front: What happened to the javax packages?
cards.back: java.* is the core platform; javax.* started as optional extensions and many moved to jakarta.*
cards.extra: That rename is why Spring 6 and Jakarta EE 9+ import jakarta.servlet instead of javax.servlet.

cards.front: Why declare a constructor private?
cards.back: To prevent instantiation: utility classes, singletons, and factories that control creation
cards.extra: A private constructor also blocks subclassing, since a subclass cannot call it.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::01 Classes and Objects

cards.front: How do you test whether a class implements an interface?
cards.back: MyInterface.class.isAssignableFrom(clazz), or obj instanceof MyInterface for an instance
cards.extra: isAssignableFrom walks the hierarchy, so it answers for superinterfaces too — getInterfaces() does not.

cards.front: What causes IllegalArgumentException: No enum constant?
cards.back: Enum.valueOf(name) with a string that does not match any constant exactly
cards.extra: The match is case-sensitive and uses the identifier, not toString(). Validate the input, or add a lookup by display name.

cards.front: Can you compile and run a String of Java source at runtime?
cards.back: Yes — JavaCompiler compiles it in memory, then a custom ClassLoader defines and instantiates the class
cards.extra: It is how rule engines and REPLs work; it also means untrusted source is a code-execution hole.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::13 JVM and Tooling::03 Core JDK Tools

cards.front: How does a lambda differ from an anonymous class?
cards.back: A lambda has no state and no identity: this refers to the enclosing object, and no class file is generated
cards.extra: An anonymous class can hold fields and implement many methods, and its this is its own instance.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::05 Functional Programming::01 Functional Interfaces

cards.front: Why is Optional often described as a monad?
cards.back: It supports map and flatMap and wraps a value, so functions can be composed over the absence case
cards.extra: map returns empty on null instead of short-circuiting an exception; flatMap avoids wrapping Optional inside Optional.

cards.front: What is the difference between Callable and Supplier?
cards.back: Callable.call() may throw checked exceptions and is meant for tasks; Supplier.get() may not and is a plain value factory
cards.extra: Callable pairs with executors and returns a Future; Supplier is for lazy values.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::05 Functional Programming::01 Functional Interfaces

cards.front: What is the difference between Error and Exception?
cards.back: Both extend Throwable; Error signals a JVM-level failure (OutOfMemoryError, StackOverflowError) that applications are not expected to handle
cards.extra: Catching Error is almost always wrong — the JVM state is already compromised.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::03 Language Features::01 Exception Handling

cards.front: How do you make a singleton survive serialization?
cards.back: Add readResolve() returning the canonical instance — or use a single-element enum
cards.extra: Without it, deserialization creates a second instance, because it bypasses the private constructor.

cards.front: What are the four reference types?
cards.back: Strong, soft (SoftReference), weak (WeakReference), phantom (PhantomReference)
cards.extra: Strong is the default; soft is cleared under memory pressure (caches); weak is cleared at the next GC; phantom is for post-mortem cleanup.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::13 JVM and Tooling::01 JVM Internals

cards.front: What is the difference between Class.getResource and ClassLoader.getResource?
cards.back: Class.getResource("x") is relative to the class's package; a leading / makes it absolute; ClassLoader.getResource is always absolute
cards.extra: The leading slash is the whole difference, and getting it wrong yields a null URL rather than an error.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::13 JVM and Tooling::03 Core JDK Tools

cards.front: Why do static fields stop objects from being collected?
cards.back: Static fields belong to the Class object, which is a GC root — anything reachable from them stays alive
cards.extra: The class is unloaded only if its loader is unreachable, so a static collection is effectively a permanent cache.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::13 JVM and Tooling::01 JVM Internals

cards.front: How do you get the stack trace of the current thread?
cards.back: Thread.currentThread().getStackTrace(), or new Throwable().getStackTrace()
cards.extra: The array's first element is getStackTrace itself; frame 0 of the throwable approach is where it was created.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::13 JVM and Tooling::01 JVM Internals

cards.front: How do you find which JAR contains a class?
cards.back: jar tf app.jar | grep ClassName, or a loop over jars with zipgrep
cards.extra: The JDK has no tool for it; -verbose:class at run time prints where each class was loaded from.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::13 JVM and Tooling::03 Core JDK Tools

cards.front: Why does a stack trace show "Unknown Source"?
cards.back: The classes were compiled without debug information — no line numbers or file names in the class file
cards.extra: Compile with -g (or -g:lines,source) to restore them; build tools often strip them for size.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::13 JVM and Tooling::01 JVM Internals

cards.front: What causes "implicit super constructor is undefined"?
cards.back: The superclass has no no-argument constructor, so the implicit super() cannot be called
cards.extra: Fix it by calling super(args) explicitly as the first statement of the subclass constructor.

cards.front: How do you read bit k of an integer?
cards.back: (n >> k) & 1, or (n & (1 << k)) != 0
cards.extra: Right-shift then mask is the shortest form; use >>> for logical shifting of negatives.

cards.front: What makes the "illegal character" compile error?
cards.back: An encoding mismatch — a UTF-8 file read as another charset (or a BOM at the start of the file)
cards.extra: Fix with javac -encoding UTF-8 and a build tool configured for the same charset.

cards.front: What is the difference between @see and {@link} in Javadoc?
cards.back: @see is a block tag that adds a "See Also" entry; {@link} is an inline tag inside a sentence
cards.extra: Use @see for related-but-separate references, {@link} where the name belongs in the prose.

cards.front: How do you write a multi-line code sample in Javadoc?
cards.back: <pre>{@code ... }</pre>, or the {@snippet} tag added in Java 18
cards.extra: The code tag escapes HTML so < is safe; @snippet adds highlighting and external file support.

cards.front: How do you convert between a byte array and a UUID?
cards.back: ByteBuffer.allocate(16).putLong(msb).putLong(lsb).array(), and read back with two getLong() calls
cards.extra: A UUID is exactly 16 bytes; the two 64-bit halves are the most and least significant bits.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::13 JVM and Tooling::03 Core JDK Tools

cards.front: What does RegisterNatives do in JNI?
cards.back: Binds Java methods to native functions explicitly instead of relying on name-mangled symbols
cards.extra: It is faster and avoids long symbol names, at the cost of writing the registration table yourself.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::13 JVM and Tooling::01 JVM Internals

cards.front: What does Arrays.toString do for a nested array?
cards.back: Prints only the identities of the inner arrays — use Arrays.deepToString
cards.extra: toString on an Object[] calls toString on each element, and an array's toString is its type plus hashCode.

cards.front: How do you toggle a boolean?
cards.back: b = !b — there is no xor-assignment operator for booleans in the JDK API
cards.extra: b ^= true compiles too, but it is a puzzle for the reader; prefer the negation.

cards.front: What is the difference between implements and extends?
cards.back: extends inherits from a class (one only); implements takes on an interface (many allowed)
cards.extra: Both create an is-a relationship; only extends brings implementation inheritance.

cards.front: How do you convert a boolean to an int in Java?
cards.back: Explicitly: b ? 1 : 0 — there is no implicit conversion and no cast between them
cards.extra: C allows it; Java does not, which prevents a whole class of logic bugs.

cards.front: What is a wildcard import, and is it good practice?
cards.back: import java.util.*; — imports every type in the package
cards.extra: It shortens the import block but hides where a type comes from, and two packages with the same class name then clash.

cards.front: How do you get a random enum constant?
cards.back: values()[(int)(Math.random() * values().length)], or a Random integer bound
cards.extra: values() copies the array on every call; cache it in a static field if this is in a hot path.

cards.front: Why is serializing a lambda discouraged?
cards.back: The lambda's generated class is an implementation detail; its serialized form is not a stable contract
cards.extra: It may fail to deserialize across compilers or versions. Use a named class or a serializable functional interface with a method reference.
